Likelihood-ratio tests between nested ctsem fits

Source: R/ctCompare.R
anova.ctJuliaFit.Rd

anova() on two or more optimised fits of nested models to the same data gives each fit's number of parameters, AIC, BIC, log likelihood and -2 log likelihood, and tests each fit against the one above it, with the chi-square statistic (twice the gain in log likelihood), its degrees of freedom (the extra parameters) and its p-value. The fits may come from either backend.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'ctJuliaFit'
anova(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'ctStanFit'
anova(object, ...)

Arguments

object

An optimised fit from ctFit.

...

Further optimised fits, of models nested with object and fitted to the same data.

Value

A data frame of class anova, one row per fit in order of parameters, with columns npar, AIC, BIC, logLik, -2LL, Chisq, Df and Pr(>Chisq); the last three are NA on the first row. Rows are named by the arguments.

Details

The fits are ordered by their number of parameters, and each is tested against the one with the next fewer, so the models must be nested in that order. anova() cannot check this. A negative statistic gives a warning, and means a model fits worse than one nested in it: either the models are not nested, or an optimisation stopped short.

When the smaller model fixes a variance at zero, such as a random effect's, the chi-square p-value is conservative (Stram & Lee, 1994). ctScoreTest tests a new random effect against the correct reference distribution without refitting.

The log likelihoods are those logLik() reports. If the random effects were integrated more exactly after the fit, by its random-effects check or a refined fit, that integrated value is used, and the heading says so. A fit with priors maximised the posterior, so its log likelihood is taken at the posterior mode, and the heading says that too. Sampled fits have no single log likelihood. Compare them with ctLOO.

References

Stram, D. O., & Lee, J. W. (1994). Variance components testing in the longitudinal mixed effects model. Biometrics, 50(4), 1171-1177.

See also

ctChisqTest for the p-value alone.

Examples

# \donttest{
    df <- data.frame(id=1, time=1:length(sunspot.year), Y1=sunspot.year)

    m1 <- ctModel(type='dt', LAMBDA=diag(1),MANIFESTVAR=0)
    m2 <- ctModel(type='dt', LAMBDA=diag(1),MANIFESTVAR=0,DRIFT = .9)

    if (isTRUE(ctJuliaStatus()$available)) {
      f1 <- ctFit(df,m1,cores=1)
      f2 <- ctFit(df,m2,cores=1)

      test <- anova(f1, f2)
      test
      test$Chisq[2]
    }
# }
